messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus is a 57-year-old single man of North American background who works as a private tutor, a role that has brought him into close contact with students and parents in domestic and semi-domestic settings for the better part of two decades. He presented for psychological assessment following a sexual assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago, when he was overpowered and assaulted by a male acquaintance in a private residence. During the assault, his arms were restrained and he was physically forced into compliance, unable to move or call out. The experience of being held down — his body controlled entirely by another man's strength — lasted long enough that he became acutely aware of every sensation: the pressure of hands on his shoulders, the weight bearing down, the complete removal of any choice about what happened to his own body. He described the event, haltingly and with long pauses, as something he had not yet found adequate words for. He knows what happened. He simply cannot locate the language.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus noticed that his memories of the assault were not fading in the way he had expected them to. They were, if anything, sharper — vivid and detailed in ways that felt almost punitive, arriving without invitation when a student's parent placed a hand briefly on his shoulder in greeting, or when a male colleague walked into the room and closed the door behind him. These sensory triggers — touch, the proximity of men, any moment in which his freedom of movement felt subtly constrained — would pull the memory forward with an immediacy that collapsed the distance between then and now. Yet the memory also arrived with gaps, sections he could not fully reconstruct, which paradoxically amplified his distress: the incomplete picture left his mind searching, rehearsing, trying to fill in what was missing, and in doing so returning again and again to the fragments that were most vivid and most disturbing.

The memories began to shape how Marcus understood himself and the world around him. He had come to believe that his body was fundamentally unreliable — it had failed to protect him, had been used against his will, and could not be trusted to signal safety accurately. He felt profoundly isolated, as though the assault had installed a glass wall between him and other people, one invisible to them but impermeable to him. And he had arrived at a settled conviction that danger was not exceptional but ambient: you never really knew what could happen next, and the only reasonable response was perpetual alertness. These appraisals — of a treacherous body, a separating isolation, and a world requiring constant vigilance — fed directly back into how threatening ordinary situations felt, and kept the memory close to the surface, never fully receding because his mind interpreted even neutral cues as potentially confirming what he now believed to be true.

This heightened sense of threat had become the organizing principle of Marcus's daily life. He scanned other people constantly — in waiting rooms, in the homes of students' families, anywhere he could not immediately assess the exits — watching for microexpressions, shifts in posture, any sign that someone nearby might mean him harm. He chose his seat in every room according to how protected it made him feel: back to the wall, facing the door. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely if he could manage it, because an environment he hadn't mapped could not be assessed for danger. This vigilance, exhausting as it was, felt not like a symptom but like rational self-protection — and it kept him in a state of arousal that made the memories more accessible and the triggers more potent.

Over the months, Marcus's strategies for managing all of this had narrowed his life considerably. He had stopped accepting new tutoring clients whose homes he hadn't visited before. He refused any form of physical contact — handshakes, incidental brushing in a hallway — and had begun scheduling sessions only with female students and their mothers present, quietly restructuring his professional life around the avoidance of being alone with men. He smoked more than he ever had, using cigarettes to blunt the edge of emotional surges he could not otherwise tolerate. He avoided situations likely to produce strong feelings of any kind. One long-standing tutoring family — a father and his teenage son he had worked with for three years — eventually ended the arrangement after Marcus cancelled four consecutive sessions without adequate explanation.

What finally brought him to seek help was a session last month in which a teenage male student, frustrated during a lesson, slammed a textbook on the table. The sudden noise and the flash of the boy's physical force — however minor — sent Marcus into a state of such acute distress that he ended the session early and sat in his car for forty minutes unable to drive. He came to the intake appointment hoping, above all, to be able to work again without dread. What he feared most, he said quietly, was that the person he had been before the assault — competent, calm, trusted by families — was simply gone.
